newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Pakistan founder's India home is a bleak symbol.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pakistan founder's India home is a bleak symbol.

text.p: Forlorn and set amidst overgrown grass beside the Arabian Sea, the disused Bombay home of Mohammed Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, is a stark reminder of his country's enduring tensions with neighbouring India.

A dispute over ownership has swirled around the stately, abandoned home of the aloof, enigmatic Jinnah ever since India and Pakistan were carved out of a single nation at independence from Britain in 1947.

The two neighbours' delicate process of reconciliation will be renewed this week when the foreign secretaries of the two countries meet in talks to sort out thorny issues like Kashmir, the Himalayan territory over which they have twice gone to war.
JINNAH HOUSE AN EMOTIONAL PRIZE FOR PAKISTAN
But hanging in the background is the spectre of Jinnah House, an emotional prize for Moslem Pakistan that has been marooned in largely Hindu India.
A spokesman for Pakistan's Foreign Ministry told Reuters Islamabad would like to get Jinnah House on lease but did not say whether the matter would be discussed at the talks.
He said Pakistan wanted to use Jinnah House, now in the possession of the Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR), a government body, as the residence of its consul-general.
Resolving the status of the building, still claimed by Jinnah's heirs, could be among the symbolic steps that could cement good relations, political analysts said.

"It all depends on how the relationship unfolds," said K. Natwar Singh, a former foreign minister and Indian ambassador to Pakistan. "But with very great respect to the building, we need more than a house to improve the relationship."
"EVACUEE PROPERTY" GOES TO GENTEEL SEED

Today Jinnah House, situated opposite the home of the chief minister of Maharashtra state, where Bombay is located, is surrounded by policemen and signs warning off photographers. The ICCR has not yet found a use for it.
In 1949, the Indian government took it over as "evacuee property" left behind when Jinnah moved to Pakistan.
The British deputy high commission occupied the house from 1948 until 1982, in line with Jinnah's wishes after he led his nation out of India at Partition. Since then it has been empty.
The Indian government first offered it for use as the Pakistani consulate in Bombay as long ago as 1977, but was dissuaded by a sharp public outcry.

Jinnah House had "beautiful rooms, lavishly furnished, and a most attractive curving marble terrace, with a lawn beneath it sloping to a belt of trees with a gap in it through to the sea," said one of Jinnah's contemporaries who visited there in 1942.
Completed in 1936 at a cost of 200,000 rupees ($5,578 at current rupee/dollar rates), Jinnah House has witnessed several momentous meetings, the Times of India daily said recently.
"Historic personalities like Mahatma Gandhi, Subhas Chandra Bose and Pandit Nehru, to name just a few, frequently visited Jinnah there," the newspaper added.
JINNAH'S HOME IS REDOLENT WITH GHOSTS FROM THE PAST
But Jinnah, a brilliant lawyer who wore a monocle and changed his suits three times a day, was unhappy living there.
"By the standards of his gilded youth the next 20 years of Jinnah's life were leaden," writes historian R.J. Moore.
"His marriage at the age of 42 to the 18-year-old daughter of a Parsi friend collapsed in 1928, after several unhappy years. Her death soon afterwards left him beareaved and with a sense of guilt."
India's rightwing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) said it is opposed to any move to hand the house over to Pakistan.
"It takes two to make gestures and we've never had a gesture from Pakistan," said BJP spokesman K.R. Malkani, who felt the house could best be used as a centre for Pakistani studies.
"Unilateralism cannot go on and on. What I say is let us wait for six months to a year and see what their response is before making any more gestures," Malkani added.
JINNAH'S INDIAN DESCENDANTS WANT HEIRLOOM BACK

But another claimant to the house is the 78-year-old Dina Wadia, Jinnah's only child. Now living in New York, she has been rebuffed by the Indians every time she asked for the house to be returned to her possession.
"It is purely a sentimental attachment to the home in which my mother spent her earliest years," said her son Nusli Wadia, a prominent industrialist based in Bombay.

"She has never stopped regarding it as her own," Wadia, Jinnah's only grandson, added. "It would be a nice gesture in the 50th year of independence for the government to resolve the issue once and for all and hand it over to her."
